Furosemide 20 mg daily was started for mild peripheral oedema; discharge planning continued with home exercise programme and tertiary PH follow-up.
Discharged home clinically improved on room air with rivaroxaban, sildenafil, ferrous sulfate, a home exercise plan, and follow-up at a tertiary pulmonary hypertension centre.
Presentation to ED with right ear pain; initially afebrile and in no acute distress, then directed to triage for further evaluation.
Triage assessment noted mild erythema around the right outer ear and moderate tenderness on palpation; no systemic illness signs.
ED consultant diagnosed acute otitis media with effusion in the right ear and arranged inpatient admission to Paediatrics/ENT; oral paracetamol was given in the ED.
Specialty registrar confirmed acute right otitis media with effusion and started oral amoxicillin for 5 days plus oral paracetamol for pain relief.
Ward round documented moderate pain without fever or systemic infection and continued treatment with amoxicillin, paracetamol, and warm compresses.

Clinical improvement noted with reduced ear erythema and effusion, significant pain improvement, and good tolerance of antibiotics and analgesia overnight; plan made for discharge later that day with antibiotics, paracetamol, and ENT follow-up in 2 weeks.
Discharge plan was communicated to the GP, including completion of the 5-day amoxicillin course, paracetamol as needed, and ENT follow-up in 2 weeks.
Presented to ED with 24 hours of poor feeding and lethargy; triaged as urgent with pallor and concern for illness.
Initial observations showed fever (38.2 C), tachycardia, delayed capillary refill, and mild dehydration; paracetamol was given.
ED assessment diagnosed viral illness with mild dehydration; oral rehydration therapy was initiated and the patient was accepted for transfer to PAU.
PAU clerking confirmed mild dehydration with reduced intake and reduced urine output; IV maintenance fluids were started and baseline investigations were pending.
Ward round identified mild hypernatremia and ongoing dehydration with continued refusal of fluids; oral rehydration therapy was continued.
Clinical improvement noted with slightly better oral intake and lower temperature; oral rehydration therapy was continued at a structured dose.
Viral swab confirmed a common viral illness and dehydration had resolved with improved oral intake and hydration.
Dietitian reviewed feeding and recommended high-calorie liquid nutritional supplements to support recovery.
Viral swab confirmed rhinovirus; patient was clinically improved with better feeding and hydration, and saline nasal drops were prescribed for congestion.
Supervised feeding trial with soft solids was successful, with good tolerance and no choking or distress.
Patient was well, playful, and tolerating oral intake; discharge was planned for that day.
Final feeding assessment showed the patient could eat a high-calorie pudding without difficulty; deemed ready for discharge with normalized oral intake.
Presented to triage with acute confusion, fever, and positive urine dipstick suggesting possible UTI; urgent assessment initiated.
UTI confirmed on urinalysis with elevated CRP and creatinine indicating mild AKI/dehydration; IV fluids started and ED physician escalation arranged.
ED assessment diagnosed delirium secondary to UTI with dehydration and mild AKI; started IV ceftriaxone and IV normal saline, with geriatric admission accepted.
Urine culture grew E. coli and antibiotics were changed from empirical ceftriaxone to targeted IV piperacillin-tazobactam.
Delirium and infection showed marked improvement; IV ceftriaxone stopped and oral nitrofurantoin started to complete treatment.
Antibiotic regimen was adjusted again after review, switching from IV antibiotics to oral nitrofurantoin for ongoing treatment.
Confusion fully resolved, urinalysis showed no ongoing infection, and renal function normalized; discharge planning began.
Patient deemed medically fit for discharge after completing IV ceftriaxone, with renal function back to baseline and outpatient follow-up arranged.
Discharge instructions and medication regimen reviewed with patient and son; 7-day oral nitrofurantoin course provided.
Pre-operative assessment for planned right tibial derotation osteotomy; mild anemia identified and ferrous sulfate 125 mg daily started with follow-up blood test arranged.
Surgical consent obtained from the patient's mother after discussion of the planned right tibial derotation osteotomy, risks, benefits, recovery, and postoperative pain management.
Pre-op checklist completed and patient cleared for surgery; fasting instructions provided and admission planned for elective operation.
Elective admission clerking before right tibial derotation osteotomy; pre-op bloods showed improved hemoglobin and surgery was confirmed to proceed the next day.
Ward review confirmed mild anemia remained acceptable for surgery; oral paracetamol was prescribed and surgery planned for the following morning.
Right tibial derotation osteotomy performed under general anesthesia with titanium plate and screws; no complications and minimal blood loss.
Post-operative PACU review showed stable recovery with pain requiring IV paracetamol; oral amoxicillin prophylaxis was prescribed and physiotherapy planned.
Physiotherapy initiated with gentle range-of-motion exercises after surgery; patient tolerated the session with mild discomfort.
Physiotherapy progressed to assisted weight-bearing with a walking frame after surgery; patient tolerated supported steps without significant pain.
Occupational therapy assessed home mobility and crutch use; patient demonstrated safe crutch use and was cleared for home use of crutches.
Medication discharge prescriptions prepared, including paracetamol as needed and dalteparin for seven days.
Occupational therapy confirmed independent crutch use at home and advised partial weight-bearing as tolerated.
Post-discharge follow-up appointment arranged with orthopaedic clinic for 17/01/26.

Pre-operative orthopaedic assessment for recurrent left knee pain and gait abnormality; imaging showed valgus deformity with distal femoral growth plate arrest, mild iron-deficiency anaemia was identified, oral ferrous sulfate was started, and hemiepiphysiodesis was planned.
Consent discussion for left distal femoral hemiepiphysiodesis was completed and written consent was obtained from the patient's mother.
Elective admission for left distal femoral hemiepiphysiodesis; pre-operative blood tests showed improved haemoglobin of 12.3 g/dL and surgery proceeded as planned.
Hemiepiphysiodesis of the left distal femur was performed under general anaesthesia with guided growth plate tether implantation; no intraoperative complications or significant blood loss occurred.
Immediate post-operative PACU recovery after surgery was stable overall, with a brief oxygen desaturation corrected by nasal cannula oxygen and analgesia given with IV paracetamol and morphine.
Early post-operative ward review noted mild haemoglobin drop to 104 g/L attributed to minor surgical blood loss; pain was controlled and tranexamic acid plus enoxaparin prophylaxis were started.
Physiotherapy session initiated post-operative mobilisation with assisted leg movements, seated range-of-motion exercises, and deep breathing; the patient tolerated therapy well.
Mother was educated on post-operative wound care and signs of infection.
Supervised physiotherapy progressed to walking with a Zimmer frame, with the patient able to bear weight on the left leg with support.
Post-operative superficial wound infection was diagnosed based on mild erythema/warmth and CRP 18 mg/L, and oral flucloxacillin was started.
Physiotherapy advanced to stair-climbing practice with crutches and partial weight-bearing; knee stiffness improved with stretching.

Ward review documented ongoing postoperative wound monitoring with mild erythema/warmth and unchanged CRP 18 mg/L; analgesia was adjusted to oral ibuprofen and flucloxacillin was continued, with discharge planning underway.
Final physiotherapy session confirmed safe independent mobilisation with crutches, and continued crutch use for four weeks was recommended.
Discharge medications and instructions for pain control, crutch use, and wound care were provided to the patient's mother.
Speech and language assessment found normal communication and safe swallowing with no aspiration or dysphagia; no further SALT input was required.
Final ward review found the wound clean and the patient mobilising safely with crutches; discharge home was arranged with analgesia and outpatient physiotherapy follow-up.
Discharge summary was communicated to the patient's GP, including advice to review the patient in six weeks after the orthopaedic follow-up.
Pre-operative assessment for end-stage left hip osteoarthritis with plan for total left hip replacement; mild anaemia identified (Hb 10.8) and oral ferrous sulfate started.
Anaesthetic assessment completed; general anaesthesia deemed appropriate and patient consented to anaesthetic plan.
Formal surgical consent obtained for scheduled total left hip replacement after discussion of procedure, risks, benefits, and alternatives.
Total left hip replacement performed under general anaesthesia with no complications; IV cefuroxime and PCA morphine started post-operatively.
Post-operative PACU review showed stable recovery with controlled pain; dalteparin planned to start for VTE prophylaxis and patient transferred to orthopaedic ward.
Post-operative ward review identified anaemia (Hb 105 g/L); ferrous sulfate restarted and physiotherapy initiated for mobilisation.
Ongoing post-op recovery with mild anaemia (Hb 10.5 g/dL) but no clinical instability; oral iron continued and full weight-bearing mobilisation planned.

Recovery continued with wound healing well, pain controlled on oral analgesia, and mild stable postoperative anaemia (Hb 108 g/L); enoxaparin planned to stop on discharge and aspirin started for VTE prophylaxis with discharge planned for the next day.
Presentation with poor feeding, fever, lethargy, and mild dehydration; triage category 3 assigned.
Blood and urine investigations obtained, including FBC, U&Es, CRP, viral panel, urinalysis, and urine culture.
ED assessment concluded likely viral illness with mild dehydration and poor feeding; admitted/transferred to PAU for IV rehydration with 0.9% NaCl plus 5% dextrose.
Viral panel returned RSV positive with CRP falling to 15 mg/L; patient clinically improved with better feeding and hydration, and IV fluids continued at maintenance rate.
Further clinical improvement with normalized hydration status, adequate urine output, and tolerance of small oral feeds; IV fluids reduced to maintenance and oral feeds continued.
Repeat blood tests showed CRP reduced to 12 mg/L with WCC normalizing; IV fluids were discontinued and full oral hydration was started.
Patient was clinically well hydrated and feeding well; IV fluids stopped and discharge home planned with advice for small frequent feeds and monitoring.
Discharge planning meeting held with parents; hydration and feeding advice reinforced and GP follow-up arranged for one week after discharge.
Pre-operative assessment for planned left total hip replacement for end-stage osteoarthritis; borderline prolonged QTc (470 ms) identified, routine bloods sent, and anaesthetic review requested.
Anaesthetic review confirmed patient was fit for surgery, recommended spinal anaesthesia, and advised stopping ibuprofen 48 hours pre-operatively.
Formal consent obtained for elective left total hip replacement after risks, benefits, and alternatives were discussed.

Left total hip replacement performed for end-stage osteoarthritis under general anaesthesia; severe degenerative changes noted, prosthesis implanted, estimated blood loss 250 mL, and no intraoperative complications.
Post-operative recovery in PACU was stable; mild nausea treated with ondansetron, pain controlled with morphine/PCA, and enoxaparin prophylaxis planned.
Post-operative day 1 review showed mild expected anemia, good pain control, and mobilisation with physiotherapy using a frame; enoxaparin prophylaxis started.
Breakthrough pain medication escalated with addition of codeine 30 mg as needed; patient mobilising well with crutches.
Ibuprofen was stopped due to gastrointestinal risk and post-discharge thromboprophylaxis plan changed to rivaroxaban 10 mg daily for 7 days, with discharge under consideration.

Patient discharged home after uncomplicated recovery from left total hip replacement, mobilising confidently with crutches and with enoxaparin prescribed for 28 days plus outpatient physiotherapy follow-up.

Pre-operative orthopaedic assessment for progressive left leg deformity; hemiepiphysiodesis of the left distal femur planned. Borderline anaemia identified with Hb 10.2 g/dL, and oral ferrous sulfate was started with repeat Hb planned before surgery.
Detailed surgical consent obtained from the father for planned left distal femur hemiepiphysiodesis after discussion of procedure, purpose, risks, and expected outcome.
Elective admission for left distal femur hemiepiphysiodesis; repeat Hb had improved to 12.4 g/dL and the patient was deemed fit for surgery.
Left distal femur hemiepiphysiodesis performed under general anaesthesia with guided growth tension band device insertion; minimal blood loss and no complications.
Immediate post-operative recovery in PACU: stable observations, mild pain treated with IV paracetamol, wound clean and dry, and plan made to transition to oral analgesia and ward care.
Physiotherapy began post-operatively with initial range-of-motion exercises for the left leg; patient tolerated session without significant discomfort.

Occupational therapy assessment showed the patient could sit and perform seated tasks but had balance difficulty standing, so a lightweight paediatric walking aid and outpatient OT follow-up were arranged.
Post-operative ward review showed the wound was healing well, the patient was mobilising with crutches, and discharge planning was initiated with analgesia and outpatient follow-up arranged.
Final physiotherapy session confirmed safe crutch mobilisation and the patient was discharged with a home exercise programme and outpatient physiotherapy follow-up.
Initial ED nursing assessment for poor feeding identified mild lethargy and dry mucous membranes consistent with dehydration; triage marked urgent.
Clean-catch urine sample collected and sent for urinalysis and culture to assess hydration status and rule out UTI.

ED doctor assessed 3-day history of poor feeding, reduced oral intake, lethargy, and decreased urine output; impression was viral illness with mild dehydration and admission to paediatrics was arranged with IV fluids started.
Paediatric clerking confirmed mild dehydration likely secondary to viral illness and continued IV fluids at maintenance rate with close fluid balance monitoring.
Ward round noted ongoing mild dehydration and lethargy; blood tests (FBC, CRP, U&E) were sent and IV fluids were continued, with oral paracetamol prescribed PRN.
Dietary assessment identified feeding difficulties secondary to viral illness and dehydration; a structured plan of small frequent oral feeds with ORS was initiated.
Clinical improvement noted with better oral intake, a wet nappy overnight, resolving fever, and improved hydration; IV fluids were stopped and oral hydration encouraged.
CRP returned at 12 mg/L with no evidence of bacterial infection; supportive care and oral hydration were continued without antibiotics.
Further ward review showed the child was hydrated and improving; IV fluids were discontinued and discharge planning began with Dioralyte and safety-net advice.
Patient was clinically well with no dehydration and adequate oral intake; discharged home with paracetamol syrup, Dioralyte sachets, GP follow-up, and discharge summary.
Presented to ED with 3 days of worsening shortness of breath and was diagnosed with COPD exacerbation; initial SpO2 89% and urgent oxygen/salbutamol treatment was initiated.
ABG showed type 2 respiratory failure with hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis (PaCO2 7.8 kPa, pH 7.30).
Chest X-ray showed hyperinflation consistent with COPD exacerbation without pneumonia; nebulized salbutamol every 4 hours and oral prednisolone 30 mg daily were started.
Respiratory medicine accepted the patient for admission and treatment plan expanded to include scheduled nebulized bronchodilators, prednisolone, amoxicillin, and oxygen targeting SpO2 88-92%.
Ward review documented COPD exacerbation with suspected bacterial infection; IV co-amoxiclav was started and repeat ABG was planned.
CRP returned elevated at 68 mg/L, supporting infection, and amoxicillin was prescribed for 7 days.
Clinical status improved with lower CRP and reduced wheeze; oxygen was stepped down from 4L to 3L and doxycycline was prescribed to complete antibiotic treatment.
Repeat ABG showed improving CO2 and pH with partial resolution of respiratory acidosis; oxygen weaning trial was initiated.
Further improvement noted with less shortness of breath, stable oxygenation on 2L, and plan to wean oxygen to 1L while continuing doxycycline and respiratory physiotherapy.
COPD exacerbation continued to improve; patient was stable on 1L oxygen, prednisone was planned to stop after one more day, and discharge preparation was initiated.
Influenza and pneumococcal vaccinations were administered as part of COPD care.
Final occupational therapy assessment found the home environment suitable for discharge and recommended proceeding with home discharge.
Clinically stable on room air with CRP normalized to 8 mg/L; prednisolone was stopped, doxycycline continued, and discharge summary and follow-up were arranged.
Final oxygen weaning trial was successful with SpO2 96% on room air and no further supplemental oxygen required.
Discharge planned for the day with no shortness of breath, no oxygen requirement, and outpatient respiratory follow-up plus smoking cessation referral arranged.
